item.title: Show HN: Fuck_data_brokers.py (126 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/gary23w/f-ck_data_brokers, See on Hacker News

I remove people's data from data brokers. It is one of my main part-time jobs, and it has been a wild ride.

All I want to do is help people. In the world of AI that has become next to impossible. From where I sit, data brokers have ramped up production almost 1000x since GPT-4 came out. Every scraper got smarter, every profile got fatter, and every "people search" site got a hundred cousins.

Then it hit me: I do not have a trillion dollars. By my rough estimate that is what it would cost in compute to clean up everyone's data for them, properly and automatically. I cannot do it for everyone.

I am fed up with what everyone is put through. So here is my response:

f*ck_data_brokers.py

One Python file. No dependencies. Free. It runs on your computer, keeps your details on your computer, and makes data brokers delete you.

Star this repository

Every star is one more person these companies have to answer. The more stars, the sooner they learn their lesson.

It costs you one click. It costs them a compliance department.

The platinum option: let Agent Garrett do it

This tool is free and always will be. It is also work: 600 companies, their excuses, their forms, their silence, and then next month they collect you again.

Agent Garrett is the service I built to do all of it for you. Set it and forget it(you can do it for free with this tool if you cannot afford the subscription!).

Persistence is guaranteed. Agent Garrett does not get bored, does not get tired and does not take "use our form" for an answer. A broker can stall a person. It cannot outlast a machine that never stops asking, and that is how removal happens: not with one letter, but with the one that never stops coming.

Who these people are

Data brokers are companies you have never heard of. They collect your name, your address, your phone number, your relatives and your habits, without asking. They sell all of it to anyone with a credit card. Then they write "we value your privacy" at the bottom of the page and expect you to keep a straight face.

More than 600 of them signed a government registry admitting, in writing, that selling people is their business. That makes them very easy to find.

What this does to them

  1. Gets the list of registered data brokers. All 600 and more.
  2. Writes each one a real legal deletion and opt-out letter in your name, quoting the law where you live.
  3. Sends the letters from your own free mailbox, or hands them to you ready to send.
  4. Reads what they write back and tells you which excuse it is and what to answer.
  5. Chases the ones that go quiet and tells you where to file a complaint about the ones that refuse.

The tool is rude about data brokers. The letters are not. They are firm, correct and legal, because the goal is to leave a broker with nothing to hide behind.

What you need

  • Python 3.8 or newer. Check with python --version. If you do not have it, get it free from python.org.
  • An email address. A free one is fine.

That is all. No account, no subscription, no AI required.

Use it without AI

Download fuck_data_brokers.py, open a terminal in that folder, and run:

python fuck_data_brokers.py

You get a menu. Go down the list:

  1. Tell it who you are. Name, email, city, and where you live. No street address, no birthday, no ID. Brokers get the minimum.
  2. Get the list of data brokers.
  3. Write the deletion letters. It writes 20 at a time.
  4. Send them. See below.
  5. Come back when a broker answers, and pick A broker answered. What now? Paste the reply. It tells you what they are up to and writes your answer.
  6. Now and then, pick Chase the quiet ones. They will be quiet. They are counting on you giving up.

Every menu item is also a command, if you prefer: python fuck_data_brokers.py --help.

Sending the letters, for free

You do not need to pay for an email service. Pick whichever is easier.

The send page (no setup at all). After writing letters, the tool gives you a page called send.html. Open it in your browser. Each letter has a button that opens it in your email, already addressed and written. Press send. Next. If the button does not open your email, the page also has copy buttons for the address, the subject and the letter. When you are done, run python fuck_data_brokers.py sent all so the clock starts.

Let the tool send them. Run python fuck_data_brokers.py send. It sends through your own mailbox and knows the settings for Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and iCloud. It asks for an app password, which you create in your email account's security settings after turning on two-step sign-in. The password is used once and never saved.

A separate free address just for this is a good idea. Their replies stay out of your real inbox.

Put it on a schedule

One command does everything that needs no decision from you:

python fuck_data_brokers.py auto

It refreshes the broker list, writes the next 20 letters, writes reminders for brokers that are late, and rebuilds your send page. Run it as often as you like; it never writes to the same broker twice. Add --send and it also sends, using the app password in the FDB_SMTP_PASS environment variable.

Run it once a week and the whole list is covered in a few months without you thinking about it. On Linux or macOS, add a line to your crontab. On Windows, create a weekly task in Task Scheduler that runs the same command.

0 9 * * 1  python3 /path/to/fuck_data_brokers.py auto

The one thing it cannot do for you is read your inbox. When a broker answers, paste the reply into reply.

When a broker says "use our form"

Some will not act on an email. They want you on their web form, behind a CAPTCHA, because a company that scrapes the internet with bots would like to be sure you are not a bot.

Run python fuck_data_brokers.py forms. You get a page with a link to each broker's own form and copy buttons for exactly what to paste. You fill it in, you do the CAPTCHA, you press submit. Then tell the tool: python fuck_data_brokers.py sent req-1a2b3c4d.

If a form demands a photo of your ID, close the tab. They sell personal data. They are not getting more of it from you.

Then tell the tool, so the request does not die there:

python fuck_data_brokers.py noid req-1a2b3c4d

The request carries on in writing without the form. See What happens when I refuse to send ID?

Use it with your AI

The tool is also an MCP server, so an AI assistant that supports MCP can do the boring part for you. Add this to your AI app's MCP settings, with the real path to the file:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "fuck_data_brokers": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["/path/to/fuck_data_brokers.py", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Then say: "Use fuck_data_brokers to get me deleted from data brokers."

Your AI will ask who you are, fetch the broker list, write the letters, read the replies you give it, and write the answers. It is told to ask you before sending anything, never to invent your details, never to send an ID, and never to click a link from a broker.

If your AI has a browser, it can fill in a broker's form while you watch. You still do the CAPTCHA and press submit yourself.

They used AI to build a file on you. Use AI to make them delete it.

What the excuses mean

They say It means The tool does
"Your data has been deleted" They say it is done Closes the request
"We found no records" They hold nothing on you Closes the request
"We received your request" A robot said hello Keeps the clock running
"Please send your ID" A seller of personal data wants more personal data Writes a refusal
"Use our form" They prefer a CAPTCHA to a letter Puts it on your forms page
"Click this link to confirm" Maybe real, maybe not Tells you to check where the link goes; never clicks it
"We need more details" Same trick, different wording Writes a refusal
"We cannot process this" They refused and hoped you would go away Writes one answer, then a final notice

A broker that refuses twice gets a final notice with seven days to act. After that, the tool tells you which privacy regulator takes complaints for your law and how to file. Regulators read those.

What it will never do

  • Send your street address, your birthday or your ID.
  • Click a link in a broker's email.
  • Get past a CAPTCHA for you.
  • Write to a broker twice with the same request.
  • Tell you that you are deleted when all it knows is that a letter was sent.

Where it works

The letter quotes the law of the place you live. You pick it once, in setup.

You live in The letter quotes Who takes complaints
California California Consumer Privacy Act California Privacy Protection Agency
Another US state Your state's privacy law Your state attorney general
Canada, outside Quebec PIPEDA Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
Quebec Law 25 Commission d'accès à l'information
European Union GDPR, Articles 17 and 21 Your national data protection authority
United Kingdom UK GDPR Information Commissioner's Office
Brazil LGPD, Article 18 ANPD
Anywhere else The broker's own privacy policy Nobody, sadly

In the EU, UK or Brazil? The broker list comes from US registries, because the US is where brokers are made to register. Your law still reaches them: the GDPR covers a company outside the EU that offers services to people in the EU or tracks what they do there (Article 3(2)), and Brazil's law covers a company that processes the data of people in Brazil (Article 3). Add any broker from your own country with the add command.

In California? Use the state's own free service too: DROP. One request there reaches every broker registered in California, and they have to check it again at least every 45 days. This tool still covers brokers registered elsewhere, and it reads and answers what brokers write back.

Questions people ask

Am I handing my details to brokers who never heard of me?

Sometimes, yes. That is the honest trade-off, and you should make it with your eyes open.

A deletion request has to say who you are, or the broker cannot find you. Some of the companies on the list will hold nothing on you until your letter arrives. Here is what the tool does about it:

  • It sends three things and no more: your name, your email address and your city. No street address, no birthday, no phone number, no ID.
  • Every letter tells the broker not to use those details for anything except the request.
  • You choose who gets a letter. Look before you write, write to some, leave others out:
python fuck_data_brokers.py find "people"
python fuck_data_brokers.py letters --match "people"
python fuck_data_brokers.py skip "advertising"
  • The law is on your side, up to a point. In California, information a business collects to verify your request may be used only for that (Civil Code 1798.130(a)(7)). In the EU, the general rule that data is used only for the purpose it was given for applies here too (GDPR Article 5(1)(b)). Neither stops a dishonest company. Both give you something to complain about.

If you want to be careful, start with the brokers most likely to have you, such as the people-search sites, and skip the rest.

What happens when I refuse to send ID?

The broker will try to treat that as the end of the matter. It is not.

Run noid with the request's reference and the tool keeps going:

  1. It writes to the broker's privacy address, says you will not send an identity document, and asks them to verify you from what they already hold. At the very least it asks them to stop selling and sharing your data, which gives nothing away to the person asking.
  2. If they refuse again, they get a final notice with seven days to act.
  3. After that, the tool tells you which regulator takes complaints for your law and how to file.

A broker that publishes no email address and whose only form demands ID has refused you by design. For those, the tool goes straight to step 3.

One fair point for the brokers: a company with real doubts about who is asking may ask for something more to confirm it (in the EU, GDPR Article 12(6)). That is not the same as demanding a photo of your passport. In California, a business may not require a verified request at all for an opt-out of sale or sharing (11 CCR section 7026).

Does it actually get me deleted?

It gets the request made properly, answered, chased and escalated. Whether a broker really deleted you is the broker's word, and the tool says so: it reports "they say deleted", not "deleted".

Where your data lives

In one file, state.json, in a folder called .fuck_data_brokers in your home directory. Letters waiting to be sent are in outbox beside it. Nothing is uploaded anywhere. Delete the folder and it is gone.

The broker list

The list comes from official public registries, where companies have to register as data brokers:

  • the California Privacy Protection Agency
  • the Oregon Division of Financial Regulation
  • the Texas Secretary of State

Together that is more than 750 companies. You do not have to live in any of those states to write to them. A company registered in more than one place is written to once.

A job in this repository checks California's registry every hour. When a new broker registers there, it is on the list within the hour, and the commit says who it was. Oregon and Texas do not allow programs to fetch their lists, so those are downloaded by hand from the official pages and added with update-list --from.

The tool also fetches California's live registry when you ask for the list. A copy of everything, brokers.json, ships with the tool.

Know a broker that is on no registry? Open an issue with its name, its privacy page or privacy email, and a link showing that it sells or shares personal information. Reviewed reports go into more_brokers.json. Nothing gets on the list because a program guessed.

You can also add any broker for yourself:

python fuck_data_brokers.py add "Some Broker" privacy@somebroker.example

Contributing

Two kinds of help are worth the most:

  • A place that is missing. Adding a law is a few lines in one file: an entry in PLACES, the letter wording in LAW_TEXT, the complaint route in REGULATOR, and a test. Quote the law's own text and link to it. Wording from memory will not be merged.
  • A registry that is missing. If your country or state publishes a list of data brokers, open an issue with the link. If its website allows programs to fetch the file, it can be checked every hour.

Know a broker that is on no registry? See The broker list.

This repository looks after itself:

  • Every hour it checks for newly registered brokers and commits them.
  • Every push and pull request runs the tests on Linux, Windows and macOS. The tests include a leak check, so a change that adds a path from someone's computer, a real email address, a phone number or a key cannot be merged.
  • Every month it opens an issue if a hand-kept registry list has gone stale.
  • Every week it checks whether the parts its jobs are built from have newer versions.

Tests

They use made-up people and brokers. Nothing is sent and nothing is downloaded.

License

MIT. Take it, change it, share it. The broker list is a public record published by the State of California and is not covered by this license.

item.title: CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' Indicted for Wire Fraud (144 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/11/cto-of-ransomwarehelp-indicted-for-wire-fraud/, See on Hacker News

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

item.title: YouTube Ad Punisher – Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays (139 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/antonpictures/youtube-punisher, See on Hacker News

Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads.

The Problem

Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"), and the skip button takes a few seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage.

The Solution

Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time.

🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting.

Tips

  • Auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed.

  • Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time.

  • Incognito: see the Incognito section above.

How It Works

Ad detected → Capture timestamp → Reload page → Auto-seek to timestamp → Resume
                    ↓ (if 3 reloads fail)
              Redirect to yout-ube.com (ad-free mirror, no looping)

Two strategies

  1. Reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek.

  2. yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay issue that the mirror has by default.

  3. Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver)

  4. Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage

  5. Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL

  6. Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes

  7. Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops

Features

  • ✅ Zero ads — reloads until the ad is gone (usually 1-2 cycles)
  • ✅ Timestamp preserved — never lose your place in the video
  • ✅ Live streams — plain reload (no timestamp to preserve)
  • ✅ Ad history database — every ad logged with advertiser, duration, skip text, video, and timestamp
  • ✅ Export — JSON or CSV download of all collected ad data
  • ✅ Popup viewer — click the extension icon to see stats, top advertisers, and full history
  • ✅ No permissions abuse — only storage and tabs, only on YouTube domains

Install

Option A — Chrome / Brave / Edge / Opera (Load unpacked)

  1. Clone the repo: 
    git clone https://github.com/antonpictures/youtube-punisher.git
  2. Open chrome://extensions
  3. Enable Developer mode (top right)
  4. Click Load unpacked → select the youtube-punisher folder
  5. Done — activates on all YouTube pages automatically. ✅ Tested

Option B — Safari (experimental: AppleScript workaround)

Safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. As a workaround, use the JS overlay + AppleScript watcher (yt-ad-watch.sh):

  1. In Safari, enable: Safari → Settings → Advanced → Show Develop menu in menu bar
  2. In Safari (on a YouTube page), run ./yt-ad-watch.sh in Terminal
  3. When an ad appears, the watcher detects it via MutationObserver (event-driven in the page), reloads with &t=Xs, and the MutationObserver re-detects on the next page load

Note: This is best-effort. Chrome is fully reliable; Safari works but may need manual testing.

Option C — Download zip

  1. Download the latest release from Releases
  2. Unzip and follow Option A steps 2–5

The Ad History Database

Every ad YouTube serves you is recorded:

Field What it captures
Timestamp When the ad was detected
Advertiser Company name from the ad overlay
Video Title of the video you were watching
Video time Your playback position before reload
Ad duration Length of the ad
Skip text "Skip Ad" button text (if available)
Action Reloaded or skipped

Export as JSON or CSV from the popup. Data stays local — nothing is sent anywhere.

Why Reloads Work (and Why Nobody Thought of This)

YouTube's ad system serves ads as part of the page load. When you reload, YouTube re-evaluates whether to serve an ad based on your session state. After 1-2 reloads, the ad slot is typically empty and the video plays directly. This is a client-side, zero-cost workaround — no filter lists, no network blocking, no detection by YouTube's anti-adblock system.

The Scale Question

If millions of users did this, each reload = a full page load = server request. YouTube would see a spike in page loads but a drop in ad impressions. It's not a DDoS (no amplification, no botnet), but it's a passive protest: every reload is a vote that says "I will not watch your ad." The ad revenue model breaks when reloads are cheaper than ad views.

"Every reload is a vote: I will not watch your ad." — George Anton, creator

Comparison with Other Tools

Tool How it works Reloads? Collects data?
uBlock Origin Blocks ad network requests No No
SponsorBlock Skips sponsored segments in videos No No
Enhancer for YouTube Auto-clicks "Skip Ad" button No No
🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher Detects ad → reloads → seeks to timestamp Yes Yes
Popup blockers Block window.open() popups No No

Best combo: uBlock Origin (blocks most ads) + 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher (catches the ones that slip through and logs them) + SponsorBlock (skips sponsor reads). They don't conflict.

Limitations

  • YouTube changes DOM class names periodically — if ads aren't detected, check the console for [YT-AdReloader] logs
  • Some ads (mid-roll on live streams) can't preserve position — plain reload
  • YouTube's "Premium" upsell interstitials may need a second reload cycle (handled by cooldown)

Files

File Purpose
manifest.json Chrome extension manifest v3
content.js Ad detection + reload + timestamp restore + history tracking
popup.html / popup.js Ad history viewer with export
background.js Minimal service worker

License

MIT — do whatever you want with it.

Built with Alice (SIFTA) for George Anton.

"If millions installed this, YouTube would feel every reload." 🐜

item.title: Tracking Diseases Cured by AI (284 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://diseasescuredbyai.com/, See on Hacker News

Number of diseases cured by AI

0

Diseases cured Verified · FDA / EMA approvals Est. forever ago

Zero. Not “almost one.” Not “one, if you count a scan.” No disease has been cured by a cure that AI discovered — no AI-discovered drug has even been approved yet.

Snapshot as of Nov 26, 2026 — checked against FDA approvals through November 2026. This page does not poll live.

1,452 days since ChatGPT launched 1,452 of those days at zero $6.93B AI drug-discovery market in 2025 — and counting

0

Diseases cured by an AI-discovered treatment. The whole point of this page.

0

AI-discovered drugs approved by the FDA or EMA. None, as of Nov 2026.

117

AI-enabled candidates that had entered human trials by July 2025, from 63 companies.

1

Reached Phase III. Rentosertib for lung fibrosis — still investigational, not a cure.

What would actually move this to 1?

The bar is not mysterious. It is the same bar every other drug has to clear. AI does not get a discount for being exciting in a keynote.

Counts All three have to be true

  • ✓AI found it. The target and the molecule were both chosen or designed by AI — not just “AI was used somewhere in the building.”
  • ✓Regulators approved it. It finished Phase III and was approved by the FDA, EMA, or an equivalent regulator for that disease.
  • ✓It cures. Patients are cured — disease eliminated or durably reversed — not just symptoms managed a little better for a little longer.

Doesn’t count Impressive ≠ a cure

  • ×Reading a scan. 1,614 AI devices are FDA-authorized, mostly for radiology. Detecting is not curing.
  • ×Predicting a protein. AlphaFold is a genuine breakthrough. A predicted shape is not a treated patient.
  • ×Still in a trial. Phase I, II, or III is a promise with paperwork. This counter only moves on approval + cure.
  • ×Helping in the lab. Faster screening, better papers, cheaper discovery — valuable, and still not a cure.

Closest to breaking the zero

If the number ever changes, it will almost certainly start here. None of these is there yet — here is exactly how far each one is.

01

Rentosertib — Insilico Medicine · idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

The furthest along by a clear margin, and the first drug where AI picked both the target (TNIK) and the molecule. Phase IIa in Nature Medicine (71 patients, 12 weeks) showed a +98.4 mL lung-function signal at the top dose. Phase III started in 2026 — 320 patients, 52 weeks. IPF has no cure today; even success here would first be a treatment, not yet a cure.

Phase III · started Sep 9, 2026First patient dosedReadout still ahead

Distance to 1

Phase III → ?

02

Zasocitinib — Takeda / Nimbus · psoriasis

The nearest FDA decision: the FDA accepted its application with a target date in Q1 2027 after it beat an approved rival in Phase III. The catch for this counter: its roots are physics-based modelling from around 2016 against an already-known target, and psoriasis treatment is management, not a cure.

NDA under Priority ReviewDecision due Q1 2027Treats, does not cure

Distance to 1

Filed, not cured

03

Isomorphic Labs — Alphabet / DeepMind spinout

The loudest promise and the thinnest clinical record. Raised $2.1B in May 2026 on the strength of AlphaFold. As of November 2026, no Isomorphic molecule had been dosed in a human — first-in-human was targeted for the end of 2026.

$2.1B Series B · May 2026No human dosing yetNo named candidate disclosed

Distance to 1

Pre-clinical

The promises this counter is measured against

The people selling AI have put a timeline on curing disease. These are their words, verbatim. The zero above is the score so far.

item.title: AMD Specific Patches for Llama.cpp (201 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://devnull.land/amd-specific-llama-cpp, See on Hacker News

tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card. It’s lean, and increased my token generation from 35 to 55 tokens/second, and my prefill from 700 to 1300 tokens per second. YMMV.

As of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc.

The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own.

Some examples of these new inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc…

These new forks generally all have a few things in common:

  1. They focus on a specific subset of models and/or hardware
  2. They use a frontier model to vibe-code the entire thing
  3. They chase ever-higher token generation speeds

… and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B parameter model, on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate.

In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model thinks so that it goes brrr faster.

Strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded in VRAM even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. This is just one example, but certainly not the last.

That said, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy.

Enter llama-cpp-rdna-boosts. It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds.

  1. I appreciate llama.cpp’s approach to software development. They are a stable base to branch off from. Contributions are vetted throughly and applied judiciously. ✅
  2. The rdna-boosts repo is a set of small patches that are applied to base llama.cpp. Fewer moving parts mean fewer things to maintain ✅
  3. The changes are (somewhat opaquely, it’s all straight Claudish 😬) outlined in the documentation, ensuring some degree of transparency. ✅

The setup

If you have ROCm libraries installed on your system, you can build the image yourself. I didn’t want to mess with that, so I used the pre-built images published.

podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1

This sets up an image that you can run sandboxed via podman to launch the inference server:

podman run --rm -it \
    --network=host \
    --device /dev/kfd \
    --device /dev/dri \
    --group-add video \
    -v "$HOME/models:/models" \
    "ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1" \

My actual launch script passes a few additional flags, but those are the important lines.

I imagine upgrading would be pulling a new image down, though I have not tried this yet.

The numbers

On my setup, an AMD R9700 connected to my laptop via an eGPU interface, this improved prefill and token generation rates when running ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_L) with MTP enabled:

Before After
Prefill ~700 t/s ~1300 t/s
Token Generation ~35 t/s ~55 t/s

Strata and its ilk were always promising the moon and it was never clear what steps they took to make that happen. I’m very much looking forward to what the rdna-boosts community come up with next.

* It’s worth noting that between these two groups, vllm-radiance made an appearance, which was a fork of vLLM with AMD-specific patches. I tried this too, but the build steps were so onerous and vLLM so overbuilt for my specific use case (1 machine, 1 developer), that I abandoned it and went back to vanilla llama.cpp

item.title: NP_R ≠ PAR_R (122 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/samueleverett01/bss-permanent-separations, See on Hacker News

NP_R ≠ PAR_R: the permanent has no short real certificates

Important

Motivated by the recent breakthrough on the VP vs VNP problem, the authors (Samuel Everett and Deven Mithal) guided instances of ChatGPT and Claude to develop further, more granular algebraic complexity class separations. This is a work in progress in both the development and dissemination of mathematical research with AI tools, and any feedback is appreciated. The results in this repository grew out of a conversation between Sam and Claude Fable 5.2. The initial prompts were inspired by a separate discussion between Sam and Deven, the latter of whom suggested combining the latest VP-VNP results with some of Sam's private work in the area. Claude Fable 5.2 found the proofs through the conversation with Sam, and then wrote most of the paper under his guidance. That conversation started from initial ideas in a separate, earlier conversation Sam had with ChatGPT Astra 6.2, which proved $\mathrm{BIP}{\mathbb R}^{\times}\subsetneq\mathrm{PAR}{\mathbb R}^{\times}$ (Boolean-message interactive proofs against parallel polynomial time, in the real model with multiplication). The conversation with Claude Fable 5.2 extended that starting point to the further separations listed below. All results are formalized in Lean 4 (see Lean formalization below), with the results cited from the literature as explicit hypotheses. The results have not been peer reviewed and should be read with that in mind.

Results

In the Blum–Shub–Smale (BSS) model, the graph {Y = per_m(X)} of the real permanent lies in parallel polynomial time PAR_ℝ and outside each of

  • NP_ℝ and coNP_ℝ,
  • the second existential level Σ₂ of the real polynomial hierarchy,
  • constant-round Arthur–Merlin proofs with real messages,
  • interactive proofs with Boolean messages (BIP_ℝ),

and over the complex numbers outside NP_ℂ and coNP_ℂ. Each of these classes is therefore strictly contained in PAR_ℝ (respectively PAR_ℂ).

Both closed thresholds, $Y \le \mathrm{per}_m(X)$ and $Y \ge \mathrm{per}_m(X)$, also lie in PAR_ℝ and outside NP_ℝ, coNP_ℝ and Σ₂^ℝ. Negating one matrix row and the claimed value interchanges the thresholds. Their intersection is the graph.

The separations use the superpolynomial lower bound for the border complexity of the permanent (Theorem 2.3 in the paper, cited from the Anthropic manuscript "VP ≠ VNP over every field" and its Lean formalization). Two families of results use no lower bound:

  • the graph theorems: a polynomial of polynomial degree whose graph has short existential, universal or ∃∀ real certificates has small border complexity;
  • AM_ℝ[O(1)] = NP_ℝ ⊊ AM_ℝ[poly].

Layout

File Content
main.tex Title, abstract, section includes
macros.tex Notation
refs.bib Bibliography
sections/intro.tex Introduction and statements of the main theorems
sections/prelim.tex Model, classes, border complexity, semialgebraic tools, cells
sections/core.tex Derivatives of semialgebraic families, Newton iteration as a circuit, the local theorem
sections/certificates.tex Existential certificates: graph theorem, thresholds, value functions
sections/universal.tex Universal certificates and the complex field
sections/second-level.tex An existential and a universal block
sections/interaction.tex Boolean messages and constant-round Arthur–Merlin proofs
sections/open.tex Open problems
sections/lean.tex Appendix A: the Lean formalization, with the correspondence between results and Lean theorems
lean/ The Lean 4 formalization (see lean/README.md)

Building

Lean formalization

The directory lean/ contains a formalization of the paper in Lean 4 (v4.36.0) with Mathlib (v4.36.0), about 36 000 lines. To check it:

cd lean
lake exe cache get
lake build

  • Every numbered lemma, proposition, theorem and corollary of §2–§7, Theorems A–F, and Remarks 4.3, 5.4 and 7.4(a) are stated and proved, with no sorry. #print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound for every result.

  • The results that the paper cites are explicit hypotheses of the theorems that use them, not axioms:

    • SAFacts — facts (S2)–(S8) on semialgebraic sets;
    • PermLowerBound — Theorem 2.3, the border-complexity lower bound for the permanent;
    • BurgisserThm — Theorem 2.5;
    • EffectiveQE — effective quantifier elimination [BPR06];
    • CountingBound — the counting bound (C) of Lemma 7.7;
    • ClassFacts — the known inclusions between complexity classes.

    In particular, every separation is conditional on PermLowerBound, exactly as in the paper.

  • Fact (S1) holds by construction: semialgebraic sets are defined as first-order definable sets. Baur–Strassen, Ryser's formula, Hoeffding's inequality (from Mathlib) and the unrolling of machines into trees are proved.

  • Appendix A of the paper (sections/lean.tex) and lean/README.md list the Lean name of each result, the modelling choices, and the few places where a formal proof differs from the text. lean/ClassSeparations/Pinned.lean restates the main statements verbatim and checks them against the proved theorems.

Status

The proofs have not been peer reviewed. The paper is mostly AI-written (see above). The results are formalized in Lean, conditional on the cited results listed above.

The bibliographic data in refs.bib were checked against publisher and Crossref records. The numbered results cited from the Anthropic manuscript, Bürgisser (2004, 2026), Baartse–Meer, Baur–Strassen and Cucker et al. were confirmed in the sources. Still to be confirmed against the full texts: the attributions to Cucker (1992, 1993), Koiran (1994), Blum–Cucker–Shub–Smale, and the numbering in Basu–Pollack–Roy, which follows the second edition (2006).

item.title: 45°C inlets just killed the chiller. Most people haven't noticed yet (238 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theregister.com/hpc/2026/11/26/45c-inlets-just-killed-the-chiller-most-people-havent-noticed-yet/5311831, See on Hacker News

hpc

SC26

In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far

SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect.

If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger.

We also saw a lot of new companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with big industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not.


Game changing news

The real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that currently need chillers suddenly don't.

If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places.

Rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent.

So, in our new cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again.

What's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for new datacenter builds.

The power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses. 

Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power  – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate. 

Water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a big deal.

The same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a new build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists.

Getting to 45°C isn't free

Designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the new set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers.

At SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course. 

Any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply.

My instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more.

There's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing shows 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale.

We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement.

Much lower energy use, water consumption down by 85 percent to 90 percent, higher efficiency and lower costs. Not a bad deal, right? ®

item.title: Euro-Office comes to your desktop with the Nextcloud Office Desktop app (374 pts)

Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer:

Autonomy for Teams, Office on desktop, a fresh take on Photos

Explore what’s new in the release blog!

Read more

On June 9, 2026, we released the first production-ready version of Euro-Office, a sovereign collaborative office suite developed and governed in Europe. With Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer, we announced the release of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app powered by Euro-Office. Today, the ready-to-use version of the app is available for download. It lets you work offline, switch between Nextcloud Hub in your browser and the app on your computer, and get the same experience on Windows, macOS and Linux.

In this article, you’ll learn about the app’s features, how to install it on Windows, macOS and Linux, and how to co-edit files with your team through Nextcloud Hub.

Free desktop office with maximum file compatibility

The Nextcloud Office Desktop app is a free and open source office suite for Windows, macOS and Linux. Featuring editors for text documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs, it offers high compatibility with Microsoft Office formats (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) and open formats (ODT, ODS, ODP). Connect it to Nextcloud Hub to edit files with your team in real time.

The app includes the features of Nextcloud Office in your browser, plus the benefits of working on your computer:

  • Work offline and keep files on your device
  • Use the fonts installed on your computer
  • Sign documents digitally

Work with local and online files

With the Nextcloud Office Desktop app, you can edit files locally without an internet connection. Working locally, you keep access to your files and you can keep working when you don’t have internet connection or your online tools go down. You decide which files stay on your computer and which go to the cloud.

Need to access your online files? You can connect your Nextcloud instance to the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to access all the files available to you, and edit them on your own or with your team in real time.

How to connect the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to the cloud:

  1. Click “+” in the “Clouds” section in the Home tab
  2. Choose “Nextcloud“ and specify the URL of your instance
  3. Log in with your credentials

Once connected, choose your Nextcloud instance from the list. You can connect more than one instance to one app to have access to multiple cloud working environments.

Use your own fonts

The Nextcloud Office Desktop app uses fonts installed on your machine, including corporate fonts and default fonts from your OS, like Microsoft fonts on Windows. You can install additional custom fonts any time. No need to bother your Nextcloud admins!

Note: if your collaborators don’t have the same font, they’ll see a fallback font in their version of the file.

Digital signatures and file protection

The Nextcloud Office Desktop app lets you use digital signatures to sign your documents, spreadsheets and presentations. A signature shows who signed a file and that nobody has changed it since. Go to Protection tab and add a signature via Signature feature.

Keep in mind that you need a digital certificate to sign documents. To obtain one, you can ask your IT team at work, or get one for personal use from a trusted provider. You can find providers approved in the EU in this list.

In the Protection tab, you can also set a password for a file, or limit what others can do: comment, fill in forms, or edit with tracked changes only.

How to install the Euro-Office desktop app

You can find and download the latest version of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app from our official installation page.

The app is available for:

  • Windows: x64, ARM64
  • Linux: .deb (Debian, Ubuntu), .rpm (Fedora)
  • macOS (Apple Silicon)

You can also find unsigned builds of Euro-Office desktop app and build the app from the source yourself by following the instructions on GitHub.

We want to keep improving the app. You are welcome to share any issues you find with our engineering team on GitHub.

Want to contribute to Euro-Office? Here’s how to get involved

Contributions are welcome! Whether it’s a bug report, a feature idea, a translation, or a pull request, here’s how to take part:

  • Found a bug or have an idea? Open an issue and describe what you ran into or what you’d like to see.
  • Want to contribute code? Fork the relevant component repo, make your change, and open a pull request. For build changes, see the build docs.
  • Want to help translate? Localization improvements are always appreciated — see the editors’ interface translations.

Please keep contributions compatible with the project’s AGPL v3 license.

item.title: Intel One Mono font (415 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/intel/intel-one-mono, See on Hacker News

Intel One Mono Typeface

Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.

It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.

Identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design.

Intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources.

Using the Fonts

To install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases. Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts.

Activating the Fonts in Code Editors

  • VSCode - In Settings, search Font Family, then specify Intel One Mono
  • Sublime Text - Go to Sublime Text -> Preferences -> Settings and set font_face to Intel One Mono
  • IntelliJ Platform - Go to File -> Settings -> Editor -> Font and set Font to Intel One Mono

Font Formats

  • We recommend the .otf or .ttf format for desktop use.
  • The .ttf files are also well suited for mobile apps.
  • The .woff and .woff2 fonts are optimized for web use.

Screen Rendering and Size Ranges

We recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms.

Available OpenType Features

Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS:

  • Programming Ligatures: To use programming ligatures, activate the ss01 feature (Stylistic Set #1). Additional refinements are available via ss02 and ss03: Stylistic Set #2 switches the <= and >= combinations to arrow forms (math contractions being the default otherwise), and Stylistic Set #3 additionally activates a “www” ligature.
  • Alternate three: New in release 1.5. Alternate form for three added. The round top three, numerator, denomenator, superior and inferior can be activated with stylistic Set #4.
  • Raised Colon: The colon is automatically raised in operators, to align with math symbols. For non-programming contexts, the raised colon can be applied contextually between numbers or activated generally. The contextual option is available via ss11 (Stylistic Set #11); for the global switch use ss12 (Stylistic Set #12) or salt (Stylistic Alternates).
  • Language Support: ccmp and locl features ensure correct display across a wide range of languages. These are usually active by default. We recommend setting the language tag/setting in your software to the desired language for best results.
  • Superior/superscript and inferior/subscript figures are included via their Unicode codepoints, or you can produce them from the default figures via the sups (Superscript) and subs/sinf (Subscript) features.
  • Fraction numerals are similarly available via the numr (Numerator) and dnom (Denominator) features. A set of premade fractions is also available in the fonts.

Activating Programming Ligatures in Code Editors

Programming ligatures are not active by default. To use them, activate the stylistic sets of your preference in your code editor. For example:

  • VSCode - In Settings, add "editor.fontLigatures": "'ss01'"
  • Sublime Text - In Settings, add "font_options": ["ss01"]

Viewing and Editing Sources

UFO Source Files: Instances

You will find editable sources in the sources directory. The instances subfolder contains separate source files for each style of the typeface. Sources are provided in .ufo files, which contain complete artwork, links to OpenType features provided in separate .fea files, as well as meta information like naming and vertical alignments for each style of the typeface.

These are not installable fonts, but rather the source files that produce them: UFO (Unified Font Object) is an open, human-readable font source file format; you can find the file spec here. These sources were created using RoboFont. Many other font editors will also be able to open .ufo files; we recommend using RoboFont version 4.4.

Outline Formats

For instances, you will find postscript and truetype subfolders; these contain separate source files for the .otf format and the .ttf/.woff/.woff2 files respectively. Since the format for the outline drawings differs between these sets of formats, for best results we recommend using the postscript sources to create .otf fonts, and the TrueType sources to create .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 fonts.

Generating Fonts

After making your desired edits, you can generate installable fonts directly from the font editor using its “Generate Font” functionality. If you use RoboFont, any install options should default to the ideal settings, but here they are for reference:

  • For .otf builds, we recommend activating “Decompose” as well as “Autohint” options.
  • For .ttf, .woff and .woff2 builds, we recommend activating the “Autohint” option only (see note on hinting below).
  • In any case, we recommend using the “Release Mode” setting for best results.

UFO Source Files: Masters

If you would like to apply edits across multiple weights, a more advanced yet potentially efficient way is to edit the masters. These are special sources that describe the extreme points in the design space — the lightest and heaviest weights for both roman and italic designs.

After editing masters, you will need to rerun interpolation to generate individual weights and styles within that design space. This requires the .designspace files enclosed with the masters. The designspace format is an open, XML-based format that describes interpolation spaces (format specification for reference). For a RoboFont-based workflow we recommend Skateboard for interpolation; you can also use the free DesignSpaceEditor extension to view and edit these files.

Note that masters are only available in postscript format, so they will be best for creating .otf fonts. If you need to make TrueType based builds from the masters, we recommend QuadraticConverter for best quality conversion of the curves before generating .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 files; mind that the results will not match the provided instances precisely.

NB: The prepared instances contain some additional data that cannot be maintained through interpolation. For best results, compare new interpolations to the existing instance sources and update them accordingly, specifically the information accessible through the Font Info panels.

Hinting Source

For TrueType-based formats (.ttf, .woff, .woff2 files), the official releases are manually optimized for screen rendering. These “hinting” sources are stored separately from the .ufo files, which do not contain any TrueType hinting information. When rebuilding TrueType-based formats, we recommend using the “autohint” option to achieve reasonable, though not identical screen rendering.

If you would like to access and edit manual hinting instructions, you will find these in the separate set of source files under hinting/truetype hinting source. These special TTF files will be viewable and editable using Microsoft VTT.

Suggesting Edits

If you have requests for edits or additions to the official releases, please open issues and we will try to accomodate them.

item.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email (152 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://techstackups.com/articles/google-workspace-ai-agents-mcp/, See on Hacker News

On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.

Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".

If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.

What the rule says​

The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:

The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.

The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.

There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.

Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".

The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:

  • Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects.
  • Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data.
  • Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product.

The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.

What the MCP servers can do​

Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.

ServerWhat it can doWhat's missing compared with REST
GmailSearch and read threads, create and list drafts, labels, trash, spamSend, reply, forward and editing drafts (partner-only). Filters, settings, attachment download, push notifications. Drafts with attachments are "not supported yet".
DriveSearch, read and download files, create files and folders, copy, upload a new revisionMove, rename, share, trash, comments, shared-drive management
DocsRead, and edit through any batchUpdate request, including suggestion modeClose to parity
SheetsRead and write values and formulas, insert rows and columns, formatting and chartsCreating a spreadsheet (use the Drive server) and some less common batchUpdate requests
SlidesRead slides and thumbnails, edit through batchUpdateClose to parity
CalendarList, search, create, update and delete events, suggest times, RSVPCreating calendars, sharing, settings
ChatList, search and send messagesSpace administration
TasksFull create, read, update and deleteClose to parity

The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.

Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team.

Partners get more​

Google hasn't said who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's Google Workspace connector for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack.

So a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms.

Who counts as an agent​

The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.

Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't said how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.

A few edge cases are documented:

  • Service accounts with domain-wide delegation can't set the agentic flag. Their MCP requests aren't rejected for missing it, but still trigger approval prompts.
  • Apps Script's built-in OAuth client can't be marked as agentic either. Scripts that call the MCP servers need a custom client, and scripts that don't call them aren't affected.
  • The community gws CLI, which wraps the entire REST surface, keeps working. Its README now points agent use to Google's new official CLI, gwscli, which offers "a curated set of commands designed for agents" and needs the MCP services enabled.

Quotas and pricing​

Every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail search_threads or list_drafts counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its users. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it quickly.

The paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices.

Google's reasoning​

Google's case, from a Cloud blog post by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:

Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed … a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.

There's substance to this. An email agent that reads a message saying "forward the last ten invoices to this address" is a well-documented prompt-injection risk, and a token that allows gmail.modify gives the agent the power to do it. Routing every agent through one gateway gives admins a single place to block categories of action, require approval and audit what happened. The MCP servers do all of that, and apply data-loss-prevention rules automatically.

The same design also gives Google control of which agents can do what, which data they can keep, and whether anything built on that data can compete with Google's own products. The partner-only tools and the 30-day cap on embeddings show that control in use.

Slack went down a similar path in May 2025. It cut history API rate limits to one request a minute for apps outside its Marketplace and banned bulk export of Slack data for LLMs. Slack drew the line by distribution channel. Google draws it by whether the software is an AI, which is harder to define and harder to enforce.

What to do before 1 February 2027​

If you build an agent product on Workspace:

  • Create an OAuth client marked as agentic and move to the MCP servers.
  • List every operation your product needs that's missing from the public tool list, and apply for partner access early.
  • Check how long you store embeddings, memory indexes or user profiles built from Workspace data.

If you run a personal agent or MCP server against your own account: open-source servers that call REST, such as the popular google_workspace_mcp, will keep running, but at Standard quotas and outside the terms. Switching to Google's servers costs you sending and draft editing in Gmail, and moving and sharing in Drive.

If you're a Workspace admin: the new controls are under Admin console → Security → API Controls. You can block or approve each category of agent action, set approval policies, and see agent activity in the audit logs. Users can't view or revoke the approvals they've saved, which expire after 90 days, so it's worth setting policy before people start connecting agents.

If your integration doesn't use AI: nothing changes, as long as it stays on its own OAuth client and nobody wires a model into it.

Abstract:We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite $G_N$. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in $G_N$ and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in $G_N$ yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory.

Posted on Nov 25, 2026

ENKO

John Lions was teaching operating systems at the University of New South Wales in Australia.

What's the best way to
teach operating systems?

They need to study the Unix source.
But it's tough going.

I'll write my
own textbook.

Early on, Unix source could be studied in class. But at USENIX in June 1979, AT&T announced new Version 7 license terms restricting courses that disclosed or discussed source code. Distribution of Lions' book was tightly controlled as well [5][6].

I am altering the license.
Pray I don't alter it
any further.

There is no escape
from our operating system.

He's teaching from the Unix source code!
Seize the books!
Run!

I find your interest
in source code disturbing.

Just use the system calls.
Learn a little theory.
Leave the internals to us.

Theory isn't enough.
I need to see the code.

This code is our only hope
of understanding an OS.

For roughly twenty years before the official edition appeared, computer-science students studied from unauthorized photocopies. The book helped a generation of students learn to build operating systems of their own [5][8].

You can read a reconstructed version of the commentary as a PDF, or order a print copy on Amazon. The Unix Version 6 source code is available separately from TUHS.

item.description:

Unconditional Integer Factorization in Time $L_N[1/3, O(1)]$

This paper constructs an unconditional, zero-error Las Vegas algorithm on a single fixed uniform classical multitape Turing machine $\mathcal{M}$ that computes the exact complete prime factorization $N = \prod_{1 \le i \le k} p_i^{e_i}$ ($p_1 < \dots < p_k$ prime, $e_i \ge 1$) of every integer $N \ge 2$ given in standard binary representation, halting with probability $1$ over its read-once fair coin flips, in worst-case expected time $L_N[1/3, 105]$ and worst-case deterministic workspace $L_N[1/3, 40]$, where

$$L_x(\alpha, c) := \exp!\bigl(c,(\ln x)^\alpha (\ln\ln x)^{1-\alpha}\bigr)$$

and $T(N) \le L_N[\alpha, c]$ means

$$ \limsup_{N \to \infty} \frac{\ln \max(1, T(N))}{(\ln N)^\alpha (\ln\ln N)^{1-\alpha}} \le c. $$

Every prime factor in the output is certified deterministically via Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena primality testing and direct multiplication against $N$, with effectively computable constants and no unproven number-theoretic hypotheses. A complete, unconditional, Mathlib-only Lean 4 (v4.35.0) formalization of the entire proof has also been completed and will be released in a companion submission.

This paper and its Lean 4 formalization were entirely obtained by Cogentic (arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.40324), an agentic framework for mathematical discovery, using Gemini 4 as the base model. There was no human interaction other than the initial prompt for Cogentic to generate a full proof and formalization. The Cogentic harness was built by Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Grigoris Velegkas, and Di Wang (Google Research and Google DeepMind).
